questions.body: What is a unique capability of TypeScript `interface` declarations that `type` aliases do not have?
questions.keyPoints: Declaration merging: multiple interface declarations with the same name merge their members.

options.text: Declaration Merging: multiple interfaces declared with the exact same name within the same scope automatically merge their property definitions.
options.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging (vital for extending third-party library typings). Type aliases cannot be redeclared with the same name and will throw a duplicate identifier error.

options.text: Interfaces can represent union types (`A | B`), while types cannot.
options.explanation: Only `type` aliases can directly declare union types (`type Foo = A | B`).

options.text: Interfaces are compiled into JavaScript classes in output files.
options.explanation: Both interfaces and types are completely erased during compilation (zero runtime footprint).

options.text: Types can be implemented by classes with `implements`, but interfaces cannot.
options.explanation: Classes can implement both interfaces and object type aliases.

questions.body: What is the key difference between the `any` and `unknown` types in TypeScript?
questions.keyPoints: unknown is the type-safe counterpart of any; you cannot access properties or call methods on unknown without type narrowing.

options.text: `unknown` is type-safe: you cannot invoke methods or access properties on an `unknown` variable without first narrowing its type via type guards or assertions.
options.explanation: `any` disables all type checking. `unknown` represents any value, but forces developers to perform type checks (`typeof`, `instanceof`) before performing any operations on it.

options.text: `any` cannot be assigned to other types, while `unknown` can be assigned to anything.
options.explanation: The opposite is true: `any` is assignable to almost any type, whereas `unknown` is only assignable to `unknown` and `any`.

options.text: `unknown` is converted to `Object` at runtime, while `any` is stripped.
options.explanation: All TypeScript types are erased at compile time.

options.text: `unknown` only accepts primitive types.
options.explanation: `unknown` accepts any value (objects, functions, primitives).

questions.body: What does a custom type guard function return in its return type signature?
questions.keyPoints: A type predicate in the form 'param is Type'.

options.text: A type predicate in the form `arg is TargetType` (e.g. `pet is Fish`).
options.explanation: A user-defined type guard function returns a boolean, and its return signature uses a type predicate (`pet is Fish`). When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the variable type inside conditional blocks.

options.text: `boolean as const`
options.explanation: A standard boolean return does not trigger TypeScript control flow narrowing without a type predicate.

options.text: `TargetType | undefined`
options.explanation: Type predicates are declared on boolean-returning functions.

options.text: `typeof TargetType`
options.explanation: `typeof` in type space queries a value's type, it is not a predicate signature.

questions.body: What does the `extends` keyword signify in a generic type parameter `<T extends { id: string }>`?
questions.keyPoints: It constrains generic type T to must have at least an id property of type string.

options.text: It constrains type `T` to guarantee that any type passed as `T` has at least an `id` property of type `string`.
options.explanation: Generic constraints (`extends`) restrict the types that can be supplied to a generic argument, allowing the function body to safely access `.id` on values of type `T`.

options.text: It means `T` must be a class that uses object-oriented class inheritance from an `id` class.
options.explanation: `extends` in generics denotes structural compatibility/subtyping, not just class inheritance.

options.text: It converts `T` into an array of strings.
options.explanation: It constrains the shape of `T`.

options.text: It makes the `id` property optional in `T`.
options.explanation: It mandates the presence of `id: string`.

questions.body: What is the difference between `Pick<T, K>` and `Omit<T, K>`?
questions.keyPoints: Pick constructs a type with only the specified keys; Omit constructs a type with all keys EXCEPT the specified keys.

options.text: `Pick<T, K>` selects only the keys `K` from type `T`; `Omit<T, K>` constructs a type with all properties of `T` EXCEPT keys `K`.
options.explanation: `Pick` extracts a subset of properties: `Pick<User, 'id' | 'name'>`. `Omit` removes specified keys: `Omit<User, 'password'>`.

options.text: `Pick` operates on classes; `Omit` operates on interfaces.
options.explanation: Both operate on any object type or interface.

options.text: `Omit` makes keys optional rather than removing them.
options.explanation: Making keys optional is done with `Partial<T>`.

options.text: `Pick` mutates the original interface `T` at runtime.
options.explanation: TypeScript utility types are pure compile-time type transformations.

questions.body: What does the `Partial<T>` utility type do to an interface `T`?
questions.keyPoints: Marks all properties of T as optional (? modifier).

options.text: It constructs a type with all properties of `T` set to optional (`?`).
options.explanation: `Partial<T>` maps over all keys `K in keyof T` and appends `?`, allowing objects to supply any subset of properties.

options.text: It sets all properties of `T` to `readonly`.
options.explanation: Setting properties to readonly is handled by `Readonly<T>`.

options.text: It removes all properties that have value `null` or `undefined`.
options.explanation: That would be `NonNullable<T>` for individual types.

options.text: It deletes half the properties of `T` at random.
options.explanation: It modifies the optionality of all properties.

questions.body: Given `const config = { host: 'localhost', port: 3000 };`, what does `keyof typeof config` evaluate to in TypeScript?
questions.keyPoints: typeof config gets the object shape type; keyof gets the union of keys ('host' | 'port').

options.text: The union of string literal types: `'host' | 'port'`
options.explanation: `typeof config` captures the TypeScript object type `{ host: string, port: number }`. Applying `keyof` to that type extracts the union of its property keys (`'host' | 'port'`).

options.text: `string | number`
options.explanation: That would be the union of value types, not key names.

options.text: `['host', 'port']` as an array at runtime.
options.explanation: `keyof` produces a type-space union, not a runtime JavaScript array.

options.text: `'object'`
options.explanation: Runtime `typeof` returns `'object'`; type-space `typeof` extracts the static type shape.

questions.body: What is a 'Discriminated Union' (Tagged Union) in TypeScript?
questions.keyPoints: A union of object types that all share a common literal property used by TypeScript to narrow types.

options.text: A union of object types that each share a common literal property (the discriminant/tag) enabling TypeScript to cleanly narrow down the exact variant in `switch` or `if` statements.
options.explanation: Example: `{ status: 'success', data: string } | { status: 'error', error: Error }`. Checking `if (res.status === 'success')` allows TypeScript to narrow `res` and know `data` exists.

options.text: A union type that only accepts numeric enums.
options.explanation: Discriminated unions typically use string literal types, numbers, or booleans as tags on objects.

options.text: A type that is rejected by the compiler if it contains undefined.
options.explanation: It is an architectural pattern for polymorphic data modeling.

options.text: A type that can only be used inside classes.
options.explanation: Discriminated unions are plain type declarations.

questions.body: How is the `never` type utilized for compile-time exhaustiveness checking in a `switch` statement on a discriminated union?
questions.keyPoints: Assigning the unhandled variable to a variable of type never in the default case throws a compile error if any union variant was missed.

options.text: Assigning the variable to `never` in the `default` case (`const _exhaustiveCheck: never = x;`) ensures a compile-time error if a new union variant is added but not handled.
options.explanation: Because `never` represents the type of values that never occur, if all union variants are handled, `x` in the default case is narrowed to `never`. If a variant was forgotten, TypeScript flags a type error.

options.text: `never` automatically writes runtime fallback code in JavaScript.
options.explanation: `never` is purely compile-time type analysis.

options.text: `never` throws a runtime NullPointerException.
options.explanation: It provides compile-time protection against unhandled cases.

options.text: `never` is an alias for `void`.
options.explanation: `void` means a function returns undefined; `never` means a function never returns or a type cannot exist.

questions.keyPoints: Narrows all primitive properties to literal types, makes all properties readonly, and turns arrays into readonly tuples.

options.text: It narrows string/number properties to their exact literal types and marks all properties deeply as `readonly`.
options.explanation: `as const` signals to the compiler that the value will not be mutated. `home` becomes type `'/'` instead of `string`, and all properties become read-only.

options.text: It invokes `Object.freeze()` at runtime in JavaScript.
options.explanation: `as const` is compile-time only; it does not invoke `Object.freeze()` in output JS.

options.text: It forces the object to be exported as a CommonJS module.
options.explanation: It is a type assertion, not a module format directive.

options.text: It prevents the object from being garbage collected.
options.explanation: Memory management is unaffected.

questions.body: What is a 'Mapped Type' in TypeScript?
questions.keyPoints: A generic type that transforms existing object types by iterating over keys using [K in keyof T].

options.text: A type that creates new types by iterating over the property keys of an existing type using `[K in keyof T]` syntax, transforming properties uniformly.
options.explanation: Mapped types (such as `type Readonly<T> = { readonly [P in keyof T]: T[P] }`) build new object types based on the keys of other types.

options.text: An ES6 Map data structure with type arguments.
options.explanation: ES6 Map is a runtime collection; Mapped Type is a type-system transformation.

options.text: A type representing geographic coordinates on a map.
options.explanation: Unrelated to geography.

options.text: A function that executes `Array.prototype.map` with strict type safety.
options.explanation: It is a type syntax feature for transforming object shapes.

questions.body: What does a conditional type like `T extends string ? string[] : number[]` do?
questions.keyPoints: Selects one of two possible types based on whether type T is assignable to string.

options.text: It selects one of two possible types at compile time based on whether type `T` is assignable to `string`.
options.explanation: Conditional types take the form `T extends U ? X : Y`. When `T` satisfies `U`, type `X` is resolved; otherwise type `Y` is resolved, enabling dynamic type computations.

options.text: It evaluates an `if...else` branch at runtime in JavaScript.
options.explanation: Conditional types are evaluated exclusively during TypeScript compilation.

options.text: It forces `T` to be an array of booleans.
options.explanation: It evaluates to either `string[]` or `number[]` depending on `T`.

options.text: It throws a compiler error if `T` is not a string.
options.explanation: If `T` is not a string, it cleanly resolves to `number[]`.

questions.body: What does the `infer` keyword allow you to do inside a conditional type clause?
questions.keyPoints: Allows deducing and introducing a new type variable within a type check (e.g. ReturnType<T>).

options.text: It introduces a temporary type variable within the `extends` clause to deduce and extract an unknown inner type (e.g. extracting the return type of a function).
options.explanation: Example: `type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : any;`. `infer R` extracts the return type `R` dynamically from the function signature.

options.text: It tells the compiler to guess missing variable types in JavaScript files.
options.explanation: It is an advanced conditional type keyword for pattern matching types.

options.text: It converts TypeScript code into WebAssembly.
options.explanation: It has no relation to WebAssembly.

options.text: It disables type checking for the inferred block.
options.explanation: The inferred type `R` is strictly type-checked.

questions.body: What is the difference between an index signature `{ [key: string]: number }` and `Record<'a' | 'b', number>`?
questions.keyPoints: Index signature key must be string/number/symbol; Record can constrain keys to specific string literal unions.

options.text: An index signature only accepts broad types (`string`, `number`), while `Record` can restrict keys to specific finite string literal unions (like `'a' | 'b'`).
options.explanation: You cannot write `{ ['a' | 'b']: number }` directly in an interface index signature; `Record<'a' | 'b', number>` creates a type requiring exactly those literal keys.

options.text: `Record` can only be used in Node.js environments.
options.explanation: `Record` is a standard built-in TypeScript utility type available everywhere.

options.text: Index signatures are checked at runtime in JavaScript.
options.explanation: Both are erased at compile time.

options.text: Index signatures cannot store primitive numbers as values.
options.explanation: Index signatures support any value type.

questions.body: What does `NonNullable<string | null | undefined>` evaluate to?
questions.keyPoints: Excludes null and undefined from the union, resulting in string.

options.text: `string`
options.explanation: `NonNullable<T>` constructs a type by excluding `null` and `undefined` from `T`.

options.text: `null | undefined`
options.explanation: Those are the excluded types.

options.text: `never`
options.explanation: It retains `string`.

options.text: `any`
options.explanation: It preserves the non-null members of the union.

questions.body: What typing philosophy does TypeScript adhere to regarding type compatibility?
questions.keyPoints: Structural typing (duck typing): if two types share the same shape, they are compatible.

options.text: Structural Typing (Duck Typing): compatibility is based solely on the shape and members of the data, not on explicit inheritance or nominal type declarations.
options.explanation: Unlike Java or C# (nominal typing where classes must explicitly implement an interface name), TypeScript considers two objects compatible if their required properties and types match structurally.

options.text: Nominal Typing: types are only compatible if they share the exact same declared class or interface name.
options.explanation: Nominal typing is used in languages like Java, C++, and Rust, not TypeScript.

options.text: Dynamic Typing without any compile-time checks.
options.explanation: TypeScript performs strict static compile-time checking based on structure.

options.text: Strict Identity Typing: objects are only compatible if they point to the exact same memory address.
options.explanation: Type systems check shape and constraints, not runtime pointer equality.

questions.body: What is the advantage of using TypeScript 4.9's `satisfies` operator (`const palette = { ... } satisfies Theme`) over a type annotation (`const palette: Theme = { ... }`)?
questions.keyPoints: satisfies validates that an expression matches a type while preserving the expression's specific literal types.

options.text: It verifies that an object matches a contract type while preserving the most specific inferred literal types of its properties, avoiding unwanted type widening.
options.explanation: With `palette: Theme`, properties widen to `Theme`'s generalized types (e.g. `string | RGB`). With `satisfies Theme`, the compiler validates adherence to `Theme` while keeping `palette.primary` typed as the exact string literal `'#ff0000'`.

options.text: It converts JavaScript objects to JSON schemas at runtime.
options.explanation: It is purely compile-time type validation.

options.text: It automatically implements missing methods with empty stubs.
options.explanation: It checks type compatibility; missing required properties still cause a compile error.

options.text: It executes type checking asynchronously in a background worker.
options.explanation: It is standard compiler syntax.

questions.subtopic: Enums vs Const Enums vs String Unions
questions.body: Why do modern TypeScript style guides (including TypeScript's own team) frequently recommend string literal unions (`'ADMIN' | 'USER'`) over standard numeric `enum`?
questions.keyPoints: Standard enums emit runtime IIFE JavaScript code, suffer reverse mapping quirks, and literal unions have zero runtime overhead.

options.text: String unions have zero runtime code emission, exact type safety, and avoid the complex runtime IIFE object generation and reverse-mapping quirks of numeric enums.
options.explanation: Numeric `enum` generates runtime code with bidirectional mappings (`Enum[Enum.A] = 'A'`) that inflate bundle size and allow accidental numeric assignability. String literal unions are completely erased and strictly type-safe.

options.text: Because `enum` is removed in TypeScript 5.0.
options.explanation: `enum` remains in TypeScript for backwards compatibility, but unions are favored.

options.text: Enums cannot be used in `switch` statements.
options.explanation: Both work in `switch` statements.

options.text: String unions consume more browser RAM.
options.explanation: String unions have zero runtime footprint.

questions.body: What does enabling `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json` do?
questions.keyPoints: Enables a broad family of strict type-checking flags including strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, strictFunctionTypes, and strictPropertyInitialization.

options.text: It enables all strict type-checking options simultaneously, including `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `strictFunctionTypes`, and `strictBindCallApply`.
options.explanation: `"strict": true` is the recommended default setting that turns on the full suite of strong type-checking rules in the TypeScript compiler.

options.text: It adds `'use strict'` to the top of compiled JS files only.
options.explanation: It activates extensive compiler static analysis rules.

options.text: It prevents the use of third-party npm packages.
options.explanation: Third-party packages with typings work seamlessly in strict mode.

options.text: It forbids the use of `async` and `await`.
options.explanation: Async/await is fully supported in strict mode.

questions.body: What is the purpose of a `.d.ts` declaration file in TypeScript projects?
questions.keyPoints: Contains purely type declarations describing the shape of JavaScript code without producing runtime executable output.

options.text: It provides purely type information describing existing JavaScript code (like npm libraries or global browser APIs) with zero runtime JavaScript output generated.
options.explanation: Declaration files (`.d.ts`) act as type contracts that provide intellisense and compile-time type checking for code implemented in vanilla JS or external packages (e.g. `@types/react`).

options.text: It compiles directly into database schema migrations.
options.explanation: It is purely for the TypeScript type checker.

options.text: It defines unit tests for TypeScript functions.
options.explanation: Tests are typically written in `.test.ts` or `.spec.ts` files.

options.text: It serves as the production minified bundle for deployment.
options.explanation: Production bundles contain executable JS (`.js`), not `.d.ts` declaration files.
